units.name: app-core
units.role: The Flask application object: builds the URL map, dispatches every request, runs hooks, handles errors, runs the dev server.
units.description: This is the heart of the framework: the application object a developer creates and configures. It keeps track of every URL route, receives each incoming web request, runs any registered 'before' and 'after' hooks around it, calls the matching view function, turns whatever that function returns into a proper web response, and handles errors along the way by turning them into readable error pages instead of crashes. It also owns starting the built-in development web server and wiring together the other pieces (sessions, JSON, templates, logging, configuration) that a running application needs. It must never let an unhandled error escape to the outside world without at least trying to produce a response.

units.name: blueprint-system
units.role: Packages a group of routes, hooks, and static/template folders so they can be registered onto an application later, possibly more than once.
units.description: This is Flask's Blueprint feature: a way to group a set of web pages, commands, static files, and template folders into a reusable, named package that isn't tied to any one running application. Code registers routes and hooks on a Blueprint the same way it would on the app itself; the Blueprint remembers those instructions and replays them once it is actually attached to a real application, possibly more than once or nested inside another blueprint. This lets larger projects and reusable add-ons organize their pages independently of a single app instance. It must never apply its registered routes to an application until that application explicitly registers it.

entrypoints.name: Blueprint
entrypoints.plain: The class a developer instantiates to group routes and resources together.

entrypoints.name: Blueprint.__init__
entrypoints.plain: Creates a new blueprint with a name and optional static/template folders.

entrypoints.name: Blueprint.register

entrypoints.name: Blueprint.add_url_rule

units.name: scaffold
units.role: The shared decorator/registration vocabulary (route, before_request, errorhandler, ...) and resource-path rules that both App and Blueprint are built from.
units.description: This defines the common vocabulary that both a Flask application and a Flask Blueprint speak: decorators like route, before_request, after_request, errorhandler, and context_processor that let a developer register behavior, plus the rules for figuring out where a package's files live on disk so static assets and templates can be found. It does not decide what happens when a URL is actually matched or a static file actually served — it only establishes the shared registration surface and file-location rules that the real App and Blueprint classes build on. It must never let route/hook registration succeed after setup has been finalized.

units.name: http-wrappers
units.role: Represents a single incoming request and outgoing response, adding Flask-specific behavior on top of Werkzeug's base classes.
units.description: This defines the two objects that stand for a single visit to the site: Request, which is what view code reads to find out what the visitor asked for, and Response, which is what gets sent back to the visitor's browser. They are built on a lower-level HTTP library and add Flask-specific conveniences, such as knowing which blueprint or route matched, looking up size limits from the app's settings, and giving a friendlier error message when a file upload form was submitted incorrectly. It must never let malformed form or JSON data throw a raw, unreadable error in debug mode without providing a clearer explanation.

entrypoints.name: Request
entrypoints.plain: Represents the incoming HTTP request Flask is handling.

entrypoints.name: Response
entrypoints.plain: Represents the HTTP response Flask will send back.

entrypoints.name: Request.blueprint

entrypoints.name: Request.blueprints

entrypoints.name: Request.url_rule

entrypoints.name: Request.routing_exception

entrypoints.name: Response.json_module

units.name: class-views
units.role: An alternative, class-based way to define a view: one method per HTTP verb instead of one function per route.
units.description: This gives developers an object-oriented way to write the code that answers a web request. Instead of one plain function per URL, a developer can write a class where each HTTP action (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, and so on) is its own method, or where one method handles everything. Flask then turns that class into the same kind of plain callable the rest of the framework expects, so it can be registered for a URL exactly like a function-based view. It must never be registered for a URL without first being converted through its own class-to-callable conversion step.

entrypoints.name: View
entrypoints.plain: Base class for writing a view as a class.

entrypoints.name: View.as_view
entrypoints.plain: Converts a View subclass into a plain callable that can be registered as a route handler.

entrypoints.name: View.dispatch_request
entrypoints.plain: Override point where a subclass supplies the actual response logic.

entrypoints.name: MethodView
entrypoints.plain: A View subclass that dispatches to a same-named method per HTTP verb (get, post, ...).

units.name: request-helpers
units.role: The everyday functions view code calls to talk back to the browser: build a redirect, abort with an error, generate a URL, flash a message, send a file.
units.description: This is the toolbox of functions a web page's code calls while handling one visitor's request: redirecting the browser somewhere else, stopping with an error page, building the URL for a named page, packaging a response with custom headers, showing a one-time notice on the next page load, pulling a snippet out of a template, and sending a file back to the browser. It also has a few quieter supporting jobs used by the rest of the framework: checking whether debug mode or .env loading is enabled, and figuring out where an application's files live on disk. It must never let a flashed message or file be delivered to the wrong visitor's session.

entrypoints.name: get_load_dotenv

entrypoints.name: make_response

entrypoints.name: url_for

entrypoints.name: redirect

entrypoints.name: abort

entrypoints.name: get_template_attribute

entrypoints.name: flash

entrypoints.name: get_flashed_messages
entrypoints.plain: Retrieves and clears the messages stored by flash().

entrypoints.name: send_file
entrypoints.plain: Sends the contents of a file to the visitor.

entrypoints.name: send_from_directory
entrypoints.plain: Safely sends a file from within a given directory.

entrypoints.name: get_root_path
entrypoints.plain: Finds the folder that contains a given Python module or package.

entrypoints.name: _split_blueprint_path

entrypoints.name: _CollectErrors

get_root_path() inspects sys.modules/importlib to locate a module's directory; send_file()/send_from_directory() delegate to Werkzeug to open and stream a file from disk.

units.name: debug-diagnostics
units.role: Builds friendlier, more detailed error messages and log output for a handful of confusing development-time mistakes.
units.description: This makes a few easy-to-misunderstand development mistakes easier to diagnose: a form submitted without the right encoding so an uploaded file silently vanishes, a redirect that would cause a browser to drop the request body, or a template that couldn't be found after checking several folders. Rather than a generic, confusing error, it builds a clear explanation and either raises it as an exception or writes it to the application's log. It only runs when the application is in debug mode, and it never runs on its own — three other parts of the framework call into it. It must never be relied on for normal, non-debug error handling.

entrypoints.name: DebugFilesKeyError
entrypoints.plain: An error explaining that an expected uploaded file is missing, likely due to a form-encoding mistake.

entrypoints.name: FormDataRoutingRedirect
entrypoints.plain: An error explaining that a redirect during routing would have caused the browser to drop form data.

entrypoints.name: attach_enctype_error_multidict
entrypoints.plain: Patches a request's uploaded-files dictionary to raise the friendlier missing-file error.

entrypoints.name: explain_template_loading_attempts
entrypoints.plain: Logs a detailed report of every folder checked while looking for a template.

effects.description: explain_template_loading_attempts() writes a multi-line diagnostic report via the app's logger (app.logger.info).
attach_enctype_error_multidict() mutates request.files.__class__ at runtime to intercept lookups with a friendlier error.

units.name: request-context
units.role: The push/pop context-local plumbing behind current_app, request, session, and g, including context lifecycle and teardown.
units.description: This is the plumbing that lets code anywhere in a request handler simply say 'the current app' or 'the current request' without passing those objects around explicitly. It defines an application context, active during setup, CLI commands, or a real request, that carries the request and session data when one is present. It provides the push/pop lifecycle that activates a context, runs cleanup callbacks and collects errors when the context ends, and exposes current_app, request, session, and g as objects that always point at whatever is active right now, safely even when many requests are handled at once. It must never let one request's context leak into another's.

entrypoints.name: AppContext
entrypoints.plain: Holds the state active during app setup, a CLI command, or a request.

entrypoints.name: _AppCtxGlobals
entrypoints.plain: The plain object backing the `g` namespace for stashing per-request data.

entrypoints.name: AppContext.push
entrypoints.plain: Activates this context so current_app/request/g/session point at it.

entrypoints.name: AppContext.pop

entrypoints.name: after_this_request
entrypoints.plain: Registers a function to run just before the response for this request is sent.

entrypoints.name: copy_current_request_context

entrypoints.name: has_request_context
entrypoints.plain: Reports whether a real request is currently active.

entrypoints.name: has_app_context
entrypoints.plain: Reports whether an application context is currently active.

entrypoints.name: _cv_app
entrypoints.plain: The underlying per-task variable holding the active context.

entrypoints.name: app_ctx
entrypoints.plain: Proxy pointing at the currently active application context.

entrypoints.name: current_app
entrypoints.plain: Proxy pointing at the currently active application.

entrypoints.name: g
entrypoints.plain: Proxy for stashing arbitrary data for the duration of the current context.

entrypoints.name: request
entrypoints.plain: Proxy pointing at the current HTTP request.

entrypoints.name: session
entrypoints.plain: Proxy pointing at the current visitor's session.

effects.description: Uses a contextvars.ContextVar to hold per-thread/per-async-task active-context state, isolating concurrent requests from one another.

units.name: signals
units.role: The named lifecycle events (request started/finished, app context pushed/popped, template rendered, message flashed, ...) other units broadcast and extensions can subscribe to.
units.description: This names the key moments in an application's life that the rest of the framework announces: a request starting or finishing, an application context being pushed or popped, a template about to be or having been rendered, a flash message being stored, or an unhandled error occurring during a request. Other parts of the framework announce these moments by sending the matching signal; developers or extensions can listen for them to run custom code, such as logging or metrics, without the framework needing to know about that code. This file only names the ten signals; it never sends them or performs any work itself.

entrypoints.name: template_rendered
entrypoints.plain: Fires after a template has been rendered.

entrypoints.name: before_render_template
entrypoints.plain: Fires just before a template is rendered.

entrypoints.name: request_started
entrypoints.plain: Fires right before the app begins handling an incoming request.

entrypoints.name: request_finished
entrypoints.plain: Fires after a response has been produced for a request.

entrypoints.name: request_tearing_down
entrypoints.plain: Fires when a request's context is being cleaned up, even on error.

entrypoints.name: got_request_exception
entrypoints.plain: Fires when an exception occurs while handling a request.

entrypoints.name: appcontext_tearing_down
entrypoints.plain: Fires when the application context is being torn down.

entrypoints.name: appcontext_pushed
entrypoints.plain: Fires when an application context becomes active.

entrypoints.name: appcontext_popped
entrypoints.plain: Fires when an application context stops being active.

entrypoints.name: message_flashed
entrypoints.plain: Fires when a message is queued via flash().

units.name: config
units.role: Loads and stores application settings from Python objects, files, or environment variables.
units.description: This is the framework's settings system: a dictionary-like object every application uses to hold things like secret keys, debug flags, and database URLs. It can be filled in several ways: from a Python object or class, from a file on disk, from a single environment variable pointing at a file, or by scanning all environment variables that share a chosen prefix. It also provides a small helper that lets a few of the framework's own settings be read and written as plain attributes on the app while actually being stored in this settings object. It must never silently ignore a config source the developer explicitly asked it to load.

entrypoints.name: Config
entrypoints.plain: The dictionary-like object holding all of an application's settings.

entrypoints.name: Config.from_object
entrypoints.plain: Loads settings from the attributes of a Python object or class.

entrypoints.name: Config.from_pyfile
entrypoints.plain: Loads settings by executing a Python file on disk.

entrypoints.name: Config.from_envvar
entrypoints.plain: Loads a config file whose path is given by an environment variable.

entrypoints.name: Config.from_prefixed_env
entrypoints.plain: Loads settings from every environment variable sharing a chosen prefix.

entrypoints.name: Config.from_file
entrypoints.plain: Loads settings from a file using a caller-supplied parser, such as JSON.

entrypoints.name: Config.from_mapping
entrypoints.plain: Loads settings from a plain dictionary.

entrypoints.name: Config.get_namespace
entrypoints.plain: Collects all settings sharing a prefix into their own dictionary.

entrypoints.name: ConfigAttribute
entrypoints.plain: A descriptor exposing one config key as a plain attribute on another object.

effects.description: from_pyfile() opens and executes a Python file from disk; from_file() opens a file and hands it to a caller-supplied load function.
from_envvar() reads a single environment variable naming a config file; from_prefixed_env() scans os.environ for keys sharing a prefix.

units.name: sessions
units.role: Defines the pluggable session contract and the default implementation that signs session data into a browser cookie.
units.description: This is how the framework remembers information about a visitor between separate page visits, using a browser cookie called the session. It defines the rules a session storage backend must follow, and provides the default implementation: packing the session's contents into a tamper-proof, digitally signed cookie sent to the browser, relying on the application's own secret key so nobody but the server can forge or silently alter it. Other code can swap in a different storage mechanism, such as a database, by following the same rules. It must never accept a session cookie whose signature does not match the application's secret key.

entrypoints.name: SessionInterface
entrypoints.plain: The contract a session storage backend must implement.

entrypoints.name: SecureCookieSessionInterface
entrypoints.plain: The default session backend: signed data stored directly in a cookie.

entrypoints.name: SessionMixin
entrypoints.plain: The extra flags (new, permanent, modified) every session object carries.

entrypoints.name: SessionInterface.open_session
entrypoints.plain: Reads the incoming session data for a request.

entrypoints.name: SessionInterface.save_session
entrypoints.plain: Writes the session data back onto the outgoing response.

entrypoints.name: SessionInterface.make_null_session
entrypoints.plain: Builds a placeholder session used when no real session store is configured.

entrypoints.name: SessionInterface.is_null_session
entrypoints.plain: Reports whether a given session is that placeholder.

effects.description: Signs and verifies session cookie payloads using itsdangerous (HMAC-based signing) keyed by the app's SECRET_KEY.
get_expiration_time() reads the current time to compute session cookie expiry.

units.name: json
units.role: JSON encoding/decoding: the pluggable provider interface, the default implementation, and the top-level dumps/loads/jsonify helpers, plus a richer 'tagged' JSON format used for session cookies.
units.description: This handles turning Python data into JSON text and back again. It provides the everyday dumps/loads/jsonify functions most application code calls directly, a pluggable provider interface that lets an application swap in a different JSON library while keeping the framework's request/response integration working, a default provider that knows how to serialize extra Python types like dates and UUIDs, and a separate, more compact tagged format used specifically to pack richer data into the signed session cookie. It must never lose or corrupt data when round-tripping the types it explicitly claims to support.

entrypoints.name: dumps
entrypoints.plain: Turns a Python value into a JSON string, using the current app's rules if one is active.

entrypoints.name: loads
entrypoints.plain: Parses a JSON string into a Python value.

entrypoints.name: jsonify
entrypoints.plain: Turns a Python value into a ready-to-return JSON HTTP response.

entrypoints.name: JSONProvider
entrypoints.plain: The interface an application implements to control how it serializes JSON.

entrypoints.name: DefaultJSONProvider
entrypoints.plain: The framework's built-in JSON provider, handling dates, UUIDs, and similar extra types.

entrypoints.name: JSONProvider.dumps
entrypoints.plain: Serializes a value to a JSON string according to this provider's rules.

entrypoints.name: JSONProvider.response
entrypoints.plain: Builds a full HTTP response containing the JSON-serialized value.

entrypoints.name: TaggedJSONSerializer
entrypoints.plain: Serializes richer Python types (tuples, bytes, dates, UUIDs) for the session cookie.

units.name: templating
units.role: Jinja2 integration: finds the right template across the app and its blueprints, prepares the default template variables, and exposes render_template and friends.
units.description: This connects the application to the Jinja2 template engine. It knows how to find a template file by checking the main application's templates folder and then any active blueprint's folder, in that order, and it prepares the data, such as the current request and session, that is available inside a template. It exposes the functions application code calls directly to turn a template file or string plus some data into a finished page, either all at once or as a stream of chunks for large pages. It must never render a template using data left over from a previous, unrelated request.

entrypoints.name: render_template
entrypoints.plain: Renders a named template file with the given data into a finished page.

entrypoints.name: render_template_string
entrypoints.plain: Renders a template given as a raw string, rather than a file.

entrypoints.name: stream_template
entrypoints.plain: Renders a named template as a stream of chunks instead of all at once.

entrypoints.name: stream_template_string
entrypoints.plain: Renders a string template as a stream of chunks.

entrypoints.name: Environment
entrypoints.plain: The Jinja2 environment subclass configured for this application.

entrypoints.name: DispatchingJinjaLoader
entrypoints.plain: Searches the app's and each blueprint's template folders in order.

entrypoints.name: _default_template_ctx_processor
entrypoints.plain: Adds the default request/session/g/current_app variables to every template.

effects.description: DispatchingJinjaLoader delegates to the app's and each blueprint's Jinja loader, which read template files from disk.

units.name: cli
units.role: The `flask` command-line tool: app discovery, dev server launch, shell, routes listing, and the building blocks for custom subcommands.
units.description: This is the command-line toolkit behind the `flask` command (and `python -m flask`). It figures out which application to load, from an environment variable, a command-line option, or by guessing from common file names, optionally loads settings from .env files, and provides the built-in commands to start the development server, open an interactive shell with the app loaded, and list the app's URL routes. It also supplies the building blocks that let an application or a Blueprint define its own custom commands. It must never start the development server against an application that failed to load correctly.

entrypoints.name: main
entrypoints.plain: The entry point run when a developer types `flask ...` or `python -m flask`.

entrypoints.name: ScriptInfo
entrypoints.plain: Lazily loads and caches the application instance for CLI commands to use.

entrypoints.name: AppGroup
entrypoints.plain: A group of CLI commands that automatically get access to the loaded application.

entrypoints.name: load_dotenv
entrypoints.plain: Finds and loads .env/.flaskenv files into the environment.

entrypoints.name: show_server_banner
entrypoints.plain: Prints the startup banner shown when the dev server starts.

effects.description: The `run` command binds and serves HTTP directly by calling Werkzeug's run_simple(host, port, app, ...).
App discovery resolves file paths and mutates sys.path; load_dotenv() reads .env/.flaskenv files; the `shell` command executes a PYTHONSTARTUP file if present.
Reads and writes os.environ for FLASK_APP, FLASK_DEBUG, FLASK_RUN_FROM_CLI, PYTHONSTARTUP, and other FLASK_*-prefixed option values.
The `shell` command opens an interactive Python REPL; app discovery dynamically imports and calls arbitrary application-factory code; commands print to the terminal via click.echo/secho.

units.name: testing
units.role: Test utilities: a fake HTTP client that talks to the app in-process, and a CLI runner for invoking commands in tests.
units.description: This provides the tools used to exercise an application or its command-line commands without a real network connection or terminal. A test client sends fake HTTP requests straight into the app and gets back a response, with a helper to peek at or change the session between requests. A companion runner does the equivalent for command-line commands, running them in-process while capturing their output. It must never make a real network connection while simulating a request.

entrypoints.name: FlaskClient
entrypoints.plain: Sends fake HTTP requests directly into the application and returns the response.

entrypoints.name: FlaskClient.session_transaction
entrypoints.plain: Lets a test inspect or modify the session between two fake requests.

entrypoints.name: FlaskClient.open
entrypoints.plain: Sends one fake request and pushes/pops the request context correctly around it.

units.name: typing-contracts
units.role: Shared type-alias definitions describing the shapes of callables and values used throughout the framework's public API.
units.description: This is a shared dictionary of shape definitions for the framework's plumbing. It runs no code itself; instead it names, in one place, what kinds of values and functions are allowed to plug into the framework at various points, such as what a page handler is allowed to return, what an HTTP header can look like, and what a function that runs before or after each request is supposed to look like. Other parts of the framework import these names so tools and programmers can check that the pieces being wired together actually fit, before the program even runs. It must never define a type that no other unit actually uses.

units.name: logging
units.role: Sets up the application's logger and picks the right output stream for it.
units.description: This configures the logger an application uses to print diagnostic messages, choosing a sensible output stream, the active request's error stream if one exists, otherwise the process's standard error, and giving the logger a basic message format if nothing else has configured one yet. It must never attach a duplicate handler to a logger that already has one at the relevant level.

effects.description: default_handler streams log output to the active request's wsgi.errors, or to sys.stderr if no request is active.

units.name: public-api
units.role: The single door into the package: curates and re-exports the names each other unit makes available to a developer using `import flask`.
units.description: This is what a developer actually gets from `import flask`. It re-exports a curated set of names from each of the framework's internal parts, the application class, blueprints, config, the request/session globals, the response helpers, JSON, signals, and template rendering, so a developer never has to know the internal file layout to use the framework. It must never re-export an internal name that was not deliberately made public.

violations_observed.note: App/Flask's core request-handling methods read and mutate Scaffold's internal registration dictionaries (view_functions, error_handler_spec, before_request_funcs, after_request_funcs, teardown_request_funcs, url_value_preprocessors, url_default_functions) directly as inherited instance attributes, rather than through any declared scaffold entrypoint. This is inherent to the inheritance-based design of App(Scaffold) rather than an accident, but it means app-core and scaffold cannot be understood or mocked independently of each other's internal state.

When a blueprint is registered, it directly mutates the target App's internal Scaffold-inherited dictionaries (app.view_functions, app.error_handler_spec, app.before_request_funcs, etc.) instead of calling a declared registration entrypoint on app-core.

JSONProvider.response() reads self._app.response_class and self._app.debug directly off the weakref'd App instance rather than through a declared app-core method, reaching past the app-core contract into its attributes.
